title: The square on the side
summary: Cut and count your way into Pythagoras, use it to measure your sensor plot's distances exactly, close grade 6 with fractional volumes, then meet the counting triangle.
materials: your four sensor columns and thresholds page from week 6
a chessboard or checkerboard if you have one

problems.prompt: Work out 25 x 16 in your head.
explanation: What stays the same: halve one number and double the other, and the product does not move.
25 x 16 becomes 50 x 8, and 50 x 8 becomes 100 x 4.
100 x 4 is 400, so 25 x 16 is 400 too.
problems.useAgain: when one factor loves doubling and the other loves halving, so the answer stands still while the numbers get friendly.
hints: Halving the 16 while doubling the 25 keeps the answer the same.
Do the halve and double trick twice and a 100 appears.
problems.socraticHint: If one side of a rectangle doubles while the other halves, what happens to its area?

variant.prompt: Work out 25 x 12 in your head.

problems.prompt: Work out 13 x 13 in your head.
explanation: Guess and round: 13 is 10 and 3, so thirteen 13s are ten 13s plus three more 13s.
Ten 13s make 130. Three 13s make 39.
130 plus 39 is 169.
problems.useAgain: when a hard multiplication splits into a friendly tens part and a small leftover part.
hints: Split one of the 13s into 10 and 3.
Ten 13s and three 13s, worked out separately and added.
problems.socraticHint: How many of the 13s does the 10 take care of, and how many are still waiting?

variant.prompt: Work out 12 x 12 in your head.

problems.prompt: A science fair board wants one honest number for three timed runs of the same trial. Say the runs came out at 41, 44 and 47 seconds. What is the mean time in seconds?
explanation: Squeeze the list: the mean is the fair share, the total shared out equally.
41 + 44 + 47 is 132, and 132 shared among 3 runs is 44.
Shortcut for a ladder like this one: the times climb by the same step, so the middle number already is the fair share.
problems.useAgain: when several runs of the same trial need one honest number for the science fair board.
hints: Add the three times, then share the total equally among the runs.
The three times climb by the same step, which puts the mean in a special spot.
problems.socraticHint: If the fastest run gave 3 of its seconds to the slowest, what would the three times look like then?

variant.prompt: Say three more runs came out at 32, 35 and 38 seconds. What is the mean time in seconds?

problems.prompt: Say a strip of card is 3 1/2 hands long and you need to mark its halfway point. How far along is the mark, in hands?
explanation: Same slice: say 3 1/2 in quarters first. One whole is 4 quarters, so 3 1/2 is 14 quarters.
Half of 14 quarters is 7 quarters.
7 quarters is one whole and 3 quarters, so the halfway mark sits at 1 3/4 hands.
problems.useAgain: when a mixed number needs halving and only smaller slices make the cut come out clean.
hints: Turn 3 1/2 into quarters before you cut it in half.
One whole is 4 quarters, so count how many quarters 3 1/2 holds.
problems.socraticHint: What slice size lets you cut 3 1/2 exactly in half with nothing left over?

variant.prompt: Another strip is 2 1/2 hands long. How far along is its halfway mark, in hands?

problem.prompt: On graph paper, plot the points (1, 0), (4, 1), (3, 4) and (0, 3) and join them in order, back to the start. You get a square standing on its corner, tilted like a diamond. How many little graph paper squares of area does it cover?
explanation: What stays the same: cutting and rearranging never changes how much paper there is, so count the tilted square by what surrounds it.
Box it in with the straight square whose corners are (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 4) and (0, 4). That box covers 16 little squares.
The box is your tilted square plus 4 corner triangles. Each triangle has legs 3 and 1, so each is half of a 3 by 1 rectangle: 1 1/2 little squares.
Four triangles cover 6, and 16 take 6 leaves 10. The tilted square covers exactly 10 little squares, even though no ruler ever measured its slanted side.
problem.useAgain: when a tilted shape resists counting, so you box it in and subtract the easy corner pieces.
hints: Draw the smallest straight square that boxes the tilted one in.
The box is your shape plus four corner triangles, and a right triangle is half a rectangle.
problem.socraticHint: What simple shapes fill the gap between the tilted square and the straight box around it?

variant.prompt: Plot (1, 0), (3, 1), (2, 3) and (0, 2) and join them in order, back to the start. Sketch it on graph paper first. How many little squares of area does this tilted square cover?

problems.prompt: Draw a right triangle on graph paper: one leg 3 squares across, one leg 4 squares up, meeting at a square corner. On each of the three sides, draw the full square that uses that side. The two small squares hold 9 and 16 little squares. Cut both small squares out, snip them into pieces, and tile the pieces onto the big square on the slanted side. They fit exactly, no gaps, nothing left over. How many little squares must the big square hold?
explanation: The square on the side: each side of the triangle carries its own square, and the squares talk to each other in area.
Scissors never create or destroy paper. If the 9 little squares and the 16 little squares tile the big square exactly, the big square holds 9 + 16.
9 + 16 is 25. And a square holding 25 little squares has sides 5 long, because 5 x 5 is 25.
That is the rule of Pythagoras: on a right triangle, the two small side squares together exactly fill the big one. You just proved it with scissors.
problems.useAgain: when a right triangle hides its longest side and the two short sides are ready to talk in squares.
hints: Count what the two small squares hold together.
No paper appears or disappears when you cut and rearrange.
problems.socraticHint: Before any cutting happens, what do you already know about the total paper in the two small squares?

variant.prompt: Draw the same picture for a right triangle with legs 6 and 8: its two small squares hold 36 and 64 little squares. If their pieces exactly tile the big square on the slanted side, how many little squares must the big square hold?

problems.prompt: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. Use the square on the side rule: how long is its slanted side?
explanation: The square on the side: the two leg squares together fill the slant square, so work in areas first and lengths after.
5 x 5 is 25 and 12 x 12 is 144. Together they make 169.
Now hunt the number that squares to 169. Your warm-up already met it: 13 x 13 is 169.
So the slanted side is exactly 13.
problems.useAgain: when two sides of a right triangle are known and the third one is hiding.
hints: Find the area of each leg's square first.
The slant square's area is the two leg squares added; its side is the number that squares to that total.
problems.socraticHint: You know the big square's area. What question turns an area back into a side length?

variant.prompt: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. How long is its slanted side?

problems.prompt: Two dots sit on your graph paper at (2, 3) and (5, 7). Walking along the grid you would go 3 across and then 4 up, but a crow flies straight. Draw the straight line between the dots, make it the slanted side of a right triangle whose legs run along the grid, and find the crow's exact distance.
explanation: The square on the side, now measuring flight: the across gap and the up gap are the two legs.
Across from 2 to 5 is 3. Up from 3 to 7 is 4.
3 x 3 is 9 and 4 x 4 is 16, together 25, and 5 x 5 is 25.
So the crow flies exactly 5. The grid walk was 3 + 4, which is 7; the straight line is shorter, and now you know exactly how much shorter.
problems.useAgain: when two plotted points need their true straight line distance, not the walk along the grid.
hints: Find the across gap and the up gap between the two points first.
Those two gaps are the legs of a right triangle whose slanted side is the distance you want.
problems.socraticHint: Where does the right angle sit in the triangle whose slanted side joins your two dots?

variant.prompt: Two dots sit at (1, 2) and (7, 10). Sketch them, draw the right triangle whose legs run along the grid, and find the exact straight line distance between them.

problems.prompt: Back to week 6. Your light column crowded near 90 with the lamp on and near 12 with the lamp off; your distance column sat between 6 and 9 cm with a hand near and near 40 cm with a hand far. Suppose you go back to the robot and log four more moments, one for each pairing, each landing right in its crowd: lamp on with hand near at (90, 8), lamp on with hand far at (90, 40), lamp off with hand near at (12, 8), lamp off with hand far at (12, 40). Plot the four dots, light across and distance up. A fifth moment reads (87, 12) and nobody wrote down what the room was doing. Which world does it belong to?
explanation: Nearest neighbour: a mystery dot borrows its label from the known dot it sits closest to.
From (87, 12) to the lamp on, hand near dot at (90, 8): across gap 3, up gap 4, and 9 + 16 is 25, so the flight is exactly 5.
Every other world dot is a long flight away. The next nearest, lamp on with hand far, is only 3 across but a full 28 up.
Closest wins: the mystery moment was logged with the lamp on and a hand near. Week 6 split one axis with a threshold; nearest neighbour reads both axes at once.
problems.useAgain: when a new reading needs a label and your logged examples already live on the plot.
hints: Plot the mystery dot and the four world dots, then look for the shortest flight.
Measure the closest looking flight exactly with the square on the side rule.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the four world dots even deserve an exact measurement, and how can your eyes shortlist them first?

variant.prompt: Same four world dots: lamp on with hand near at (90, 8), lamp on with hand far at (90, 40), lamp off with hand near at (12, 8), lamp off with hand far at (12, 40). A mystery moment lands at (15, 36). Sketch all five dots on graph paper. Which world does it belong to?

problems.prompt: A mystery dot sits at (24, 20). Two logged dots offer it their labels: A at (12, 8) and B at (12, 40). True or false: B is the nearer neighbour.
explanation: Nearest neighbour turns exact with the square on the side, and here is the time saver: to compare two flights, compare their squared totals and skip the last step.
To A: across 12, up 12. 144 + 144 is 288.
To B: across 12, up 20. 144 + 400 is 544.
288 is smaller, so A is nearer and the claim is false. Nobody needed a square root: whichever squared total is smaller, that flight is shorter, guaranteed.
problems.useAgain: when two candidate neighbours both look close and only exact measuring can crown one.
hints: Work out across gap squared plus up gap squared for each candidate.
Before computing, ask what is the same about the two flights and what actually differs.
problems.socraticHint: Could you crown the nearer neighbour here without finishing both squared totals? What lets you?

variant.prompt: A mystery dot sits at (24, 32), with the same two logged dots: A at (12, 8) and B at (12, 40). True or false: B is the nearer neighbour.

problems.prompt:
Talia found the volume of a box measuring 6 cm by 1 1/2 cm by 2 cm.
Line 1: Of means times: volume is edge times edge times edge.
Line 2: Multiply 6 by 1 1/2 first: six one-and-a-halfs make 9.
Line 3: Then multiply that 9 by the last edge, 2.
Line 4: 9 times 2 is 16.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 through 3 are correct: 6 times 1 1/2 is 9, and that 9 still needs multiplying by the last edge, 2.
Line 4 is wrong: 9 times 2 is 18, not 16.
Of means times: every edge takes part in one multiplication, fractions included.
The box's true volume is 18 cubic centimeters.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction multiplication step is right but the final whole-number multiplication still needs its own check.
hints: Recompute every line's own multiplication yourself, fractions included.
Of means times: every edge, whole number or mixed number, takes part in one multiplication, done fully before moving to the next.
problems.socraticHint: Does the fraction multiplication in this working actually come out to the number claimed?

variant.prompt:
Rowan found the volume of a box measuring 4 cm by 1 1/2 cm by 3 cm.
Line 1: Of means times: volume is edge times edge times edge.
Line 2: Multiply 4 by 1 1/2 first: four one-and-a-halfs make 5.
Line 3: Then multiply that 5 by the last edge, 3.
Line 4: 5 times 3 is 15.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Little cubes with 1/2 cm edges are packed into a box 3 cm by 2 cm by 1 1/2 cm, with no gaps. How many little cubes fill the box exactly?
explanation: Same slice: measure everything in the little cube's own unit. A 1/2 cm cube fits 2 to a centimeter.
Along 3 cm stand 6 cubes, along 2 cm stand 4, and along 1 1/2 cm stand 3.
6 x 4 x 3 is 72 little cubes.
Check it by volume: the box holds 3 x 2 x 1 1/2, which is 9 cubic cm, and each little cube is 1/8 of a cubic cm, so 9 x 8 gives 72 again. Two roads, one answer, and grade 6 volume closes here.
problems.useAgain: when a box and its filler cubes speak different sizes, so you remeasure the box in the filler's own unit.
hints: How many half centimeter cubes stand shoulder to shoulder in one single centimeter?
Count cubes along each edge separately, then multiply the three counts.
problems.socraticHint: The 1 1/2 cm edge held no whole centimeter cube. Why does it hold a whole number of these little ones?

variant.prompt: The same 1/2 cm cubes are packed into a box 2 cm by 2 cm by 2 1/2 cm, with no gaps. How many little cubes fill it exactly?

steps.title: Four quadrants read at a glance, and one more shuffled deck

problems.prompt: Point (-3, 4) is plotted on a coordinate grid. Which quadrant is it in: 1, 2, 3 or 4?
explanation: Quadrant 1 is positive x and positive y; quadrant 2 is negative x and positive y.
Here x is -3 (negative) and y is 4 (positive), which matches quadrant 2.
problems.useAgain: when a point's quadrant needs naming from the signs of its x and y coordinates alone.
hints: Is the x-coordinate positive or negative? What about the y-coordinate?
Match those two signs to the quadrant that has exactly that combination.
problems.socraticHint: Which quadrant is the only one with a negative x and a positive y?

variant.prompt: Point (5, -2) is plotted on a coordinate grid. Which quadrant is it in: 1, 2, 3 or 4?

problems.prompt: A point lies in quadrant 3, with an x-coordinate of -6. True or false: its y-coordinate must be negative.
explanation: Quadrant 3 is where both coordinates are negative.
Since the point is in quadrant 3, its y-coordinate has to be negative too, no matter what the x-coordinate's exact value is.
problems.useAgain: when a point's quadrant is known and one coordinate's sign needs reasoning out for the other.
hints: What are the signs of both coordinates in quadrant 3?
The exact x-value does not change what quadrant 3 requires of the y-value's sign.
problems.socraticHint: Does knowing only the exact x-value of a point tell you anything, if you already know which quadrant it is in?

variant.prompt: A point lies in quadrant 2, with an x-coordinate of -4. True or false: its y-coordinate must be negative.

problems.prompt: A stack of cards numbered 1 to 10 is shuffled. One card is drawn at random. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, that the number is a multiple of 4?
explanation: The multiples of 4 from 1 to 10 are 4 and 8, which is 2 cards.
2 out of 10 simplifies to 1/5.
problems.useAgain: when a probability comes from counting how many numbers in a range fit a multiple rule.
hints: List every multiple of 4 between 1 and 10.
Put that count over the total 10 cards, then simplify.
problems.socraticHint: Is 10 itself a multiple of 4?

variant.prompt: A stack of cards numbered 1 to 10 is shuffled. One card is drawn at random. What is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, that the number is a multiple of 3?

problems.prompt: Using the same stack of cards numbered 1 to 10, what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of drawing a number greater than 7?
explanation: The numbers greater than 7 in this stack are 8, 9 and 10, which is 3 cards.
3 out of 10 is already in lowest terms.
problems.useAgain: when a probability comes from counting numbers above or below a cutoff in a range.
hints: List every number in the stack greater than 7.
Put that count over the total 10 cards.
problems.socraticHint: Does greater than 7 include the number 7 itself?

variant.prompt: Using the same stack of cards numbered 1 to 10, what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of drawing an even number?

problems.prompt: Build this triangle on paper. Row 0 is just 1. Row 1 is 1, 1. Row 2 is 1, 2, 1. Row 3 is 1, 3, 3, 1. Row 4 is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. Every row starts and ends with 1. Find the rule that makes the inside numbers, then write row 5. What number sits directly below the 4 and the 6?
explanation: Find the rule: each inside number is the sum of the two numbers sitting above it.
Check it on what you can already see: 2 is 1 + 1, each 3 is 1 + 2, the 6 is 3 + 3, each 4 is 1 + 3.
So below the 4 and the 6 sits 4 + 6, which is 10, and row 5 reads 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1.
This is Pascal's triangle. This week it will count handshakes, walks and coin flips without ever listing them.
problems.useAgain: when a number pattern grows row by row and each new entry looks built from its neighbours.
hints: Compare each inside number with the two numbers sitting above it.
Test your rule on the 6 in row 4 before trusting it further down.
problems.socraticHint: What could the two numbers above an entry have to do with the entry itself? Make a guess and test it on row 3.

variant.prompt: Same triangle. Row 5 is 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. What number sits directly below the 5 and the first 10?

problems.prompt: Add up each full row of Pascal's triangle: row 0 gives 1, row 1 gives 2, row 2 gives 1 + 2 + 1 which is 4, row 3 gives 8. The row sums are marching somewhere familiar. What do all the numbers in row 6 add up to?
explanation: Exponents fast forward: the sums 1, 2, 4, 8 double at every row, so row 6 is 2 multiplied by itself 6 times.
Why doubling: every number in a row gets added into two different entries of the next row, once to its left child and once to its right child, so the next row's total counts everything exactly twice.
Keep doubling: row 4 gives 16, row 5 gives 32, row 6 gives 64.
You met this staircase in week 9: stacked doubling grows monstrous fast.
problems.useAgain: when a total doubles at every step and you want a far step without adding up the middle ones.
hints: Work out the sums of the first few rows and line them up.
Ask where each number of a row ends up inside the row below it.
problems.socraticHint: Each number in a row feeds how many entries of the row below, and what does that do to the row total?

variant.prompt: Same triangle, same march. What do all the numbers in row 8 add up to?

problems.prompt: Invent your own choose-2 counting problem, like the science fair handshakes: pick your own group size and your own pairing action (handshakes, matches, routes, anything where every pair of people or things is counted exactly once). Find your answer two ways, once by reading the matching diagonal of Pascal's triangle and once using the choices-multiply idea directly, and show both ways agree.
explanation: Pick your own group size first, for example 6 people at a chess club where every pair plays exactly one game.
Read Pascal's triangle: the third diagonal, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, counts pairs for groups of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
So 6 people gives 15 games.
Check with choices-multiply: 6 people give 6 times 5 ways to pick an ordered pair, but each game is counted twice that way.
Divide by 2 to undo the double count, which is also 15.
Both ways agreeing is the whole point: two different roads to the same number is real proof, not luck.
problems.useAgain: when you want to invent your own choose-2 counting problem and check it two different ways.
hints: Pick your group size first, then find it on Pascal's triangle diagonal before trying the multiplication method.
Choices-multiply counts every pair exactly twice, once each direction; dividing by 2 fixes that.
problems.socraticHint: Why does every pair get counted exactly twice by the ordered-choice method, no matter what the group size is?

problems.prompt: Week 9's walks return. A town's streets make a grid of blocks, 2 blocks wide and 2 blocks tall. You start at the top left corner and walk to the bottom right corner, moving only right or down along the streets. How many different shortest walks are there?
explanation: Label every street corner with how many walks can reach it, starting with 1 at home.
A corner can only be entered from its left or from above, so its count is the left corner's count plus the above corner's count. That is exactly the triangle's adding rule.
Fill the corners in: the top edge and left edge all read 1, the middle reads 2, the next corners read 3, and the bottom right corner collects 3 + 3, which is 6.
Tilt your head 45 degrees and the labeled grid is Pascal's triangle. The middle of row 4, the number 6, was sitting there waiting.
problems.useAgain: when walks through a grid need counting and every corner can only be entered from two sides.
hints: Write at each corner how many walks can reach it, starting with 1 at home.
A corner's count comes only from the two corners that can feed it.
problems.socraticHint: From which corners can a walker take the final step into any given corner, and what does that make the corner's count?

variant.prompt: The grid shrinks: 2 blocks wide and 1 block tall. Moving only right or down, how many different shortest walks go from the top left corner to the bottom right corner?

problems.prompt: Flip a fair coin 4 times and write down the heads and tails in order. Week 9's counting says there are 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, which is 16, possible records. Row 4 of the triangle reads 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. How many of the 16 records show exactly 2 heads?
explanation: Choices multiply gave the total: two choices per flip, four flips, 16 records in all.
Sort the 16 records into piles by how many heads they hold: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4. Row 4 counts the piles: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.
The middle entry says 6 records hold exactly 2 heads. Doubt it? List them: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH.
So the chance of exactly 2 heads is 6 out of 16, which is 3 out of 8. Last week's favorable over total, now read straight off a row.
problems.useAgain: when flip style records need sorting by how many of one kind they hold.
hints: The total of 16 is already done; the question asks about one pile of the sorting.
Row 4 has five numbers and there are five possible head counts. Match them up in order.
problems.socraticHint: Why should the pile with exactly 2 heads be the biggest of the five piles?

variant.prompt: Same 4 flips, same 16 records, same row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. How many of the 16 records show exactly 3 heads?

problems.prompt: Write why the adding rule must be true, using walks. Do the domino proof's two jobs. First job: say why the corner you start from carries the count 1. Second job: explain why the number of shortest walks to any other corner equals the count at the corner on its left plus the count at the corner above it, with no walk missed and no walk counted twice.

mustMention: only two ways to enter a corner

explanation: First domino: the start corner is reached by exactly one walk, the walk going nowhere, so its count is 1 before any rule runs.
Look only at the last step of a walk arriving at a corner. Moving only right or down, that step came from the left neighbour or the one above: no third door.
The walks arriving through the left door are exactly the walks that reached the left corner, one each. Same for the door above.
A walk cannot use both doors at once, so no walk is counted twice, and every walk uses one of them, so none is missed.
So the corner's count is the left count plus the above count, built honestly all the way back to the single walk sitting at home. That is Pascal's adding rule wearing street clothes.
problems.useAgain: when a count builds level by level and you must argue every case enters through exactly one door.
hints: Settle the corner you start from first, before any adding rule is allowed to run.
Split all the arriving walks into piles by that last step.
problems.socraticHint: What are the only possible last steps of a shortest walk arriving at a corner?

variant.prompt: Same adding rule, told with coin flips instead of streets. Explain why the number of 4 flip records holding exactly 2 heads equals the number of 3 flip records holding 2 heads plus the number of 3 flip records holding 1 head.

mustMention: look only at the last flip, heads or tails
2 heads in 4 flips is 2 heads in the first 3 then tails, or 1 head in the first 3 then heads
no record lands in both piles

steps.title: The monster problem: squares on the chessboard

problems.prompt: The month 3 monster. A chessboard is an 8 by 8 grid of small squares. Count every square that can be traced along its lines: all the 1 by 1 squares, all the 2 by 2 squares, all the way up to the whole 8 by 8 board. How many squares are there in total, and how do you know none escaped your count?

mustMention: count one size at a time

explanation: Count one size at a time, and let week 9's choices multiply count each size: a square is pinned by its top left corner, so count the places that corner can sit.
A 1 by 1 square's corner can sit in 8 columns and 8 rows: 8 x 8 is 64. A 2 by 2 square needs one more column and one more row of room, so its corner has only 7 x 7 places: 49.
Each size up loses one column and one row of freedom: 6 x 6 places for the 3 by 3 squares, then 25, 16, 9, 4, and a single place for the whole board.
The counts are the square numbers in reverse: 64, 49, 36, 25, 16, 9, 4, 1.
Added up: 64 + 49 is 113, plus 36 is 149, plus 25 is 174, plus 16 is 190, plus 9 is 199, plus 4 is 203, plus 1 is 204.
Every square on the board has exactly one size, so it landed in exactly one pile: nothing missed, nothing counted twice. The total is 204.
problems.useAgain: when a monstrous count splits into sizes and each size falls to a rows times columns count of its own.
hints: Do not count squares one by one; count one size at a time, starting with the smallest.
Pin each square by its top left corner and ask where that corner is allowed to sit.
problems.socraticHint: How many places can the top left corner of a 2 by 2 square sit, and what happens to that freedom as the squares grow?

variant.prompt: The same monster on a smaller board: a 4 by 4 board of small squares. How many squares of every size can be traced on its lines, and how do you know your count missed none?

mustMention: count one size at a time

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write the scissors story: why must the two small squares of your 3, 4, 5 triangle exactly fill the big one, and what does that rule let you measure that a ruler laid along the grid lines never could?

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Record yourself teaching the adding rule as a domino proof: start with the first domino, the single walk sitting at the corner you start from, then give the two doors argument for why every other corner's count is the left count plus the above count. End with your favourite thing the triangle counted this week.
